explain.say: A harbour needs calm water so ships can load safely, but storm waves carry enormous energy. A breakwater is a long wall or mound built out into the sea to take the waves' blows.

faq.a: A breakwater is a barrier built out into the sea that takes the force of the waves. It breaks them up and soaks up their energy, so the water behind it, in the harbour, stays calm.
asks: How are harbours protected from waves?

faq.a: Tetrapods are concrete blocks with four stubby legs that interlock on the face of a breakwater. Their gaps let waves pour in and lose energy, and they are hard for waves to dislodge.
asks: Why are there concrete blocks on harbour walls?

faq.a: Most are rubble mounds: a core of quarry stone, covered by layers of bigger rocks and finally the heavy armour layer. Each layer stops the one below from washing out.
asks: What is a rubble mound breakwater?

faq.q: Why do harbours need calm water?
faq.a: Ships moored in waves would bang against the quay and each other, and loading cargo or passengers would be dangerous. A breakwater shelters the area so work can carry on in rough weather.

faq.q: Why don't breakwaters just use a smooth wall?
faq.a: Some do, but waves hitting a smooth vertical wall bounce back and can scour the seabed at its foot. A rough, sloping mound absorbs energy instead of reflecting it.

facts: The tetrapod armour unit was invented in France in 1950 by Pierre Danel and Paul Anglès d'Auriac.
Rough, porous breakwater faces absorb wave energy as turbulence and reflect far less of it than smooth walls.
